group.passage:
Coming-of-age, or the transition from a teenager into an adult, is a significant landmark in people’s lives around the world. Yet, how and when it is celebrated as a rite of passage varies with different cultures and countries.
For Apache, a Native American tribe, coming-of-age rituals, also called the “Sunrise Ceremony,” are tailor-made for girls. Every fourth of July, girls are covered in pollen and spend four days praying, dancing, singing, and chanting. While this may sound like a lot of fun, it actually is quite challenging—they have to hold curved poles while dancing in place to the music for more than ten hours with no rests. Girls who make it to the end are believed to be gifted with the strength, endurance, and character required of womanhood.
In Tanzania and Kenya, Maasai boys aged between 10-20 go through several tests to be recognized as men. After a night of stay in the wild by themselves, the boys will be circumcised (removing the loose skin of a boy’s penis) to mark their formal transition into manhood. During this process, the boys are not expected to cry or flinch; otherwise, they will be deemed cowards. Afterwards, the boys will live in the warrior camp learning skills for the next ten years before finally being granted the title of “senior warriors” and allowed to marry.
In Brazilian Amazon, when boys in an indigenous tribe turn 13, they have to wear a special kind of gloves. They will be first led into the jungle and collect the bullet ants, which will then be sedated and woven into the gloves with their stingers pointed inward. As the name suggests, a sting by the bullet ants can cause pain comparable to that by a real bullet! The boys will have to wear the gloves for ten minutes up to twenty times over the span of several months, an experience believed to be crucial for survival in the rainforest.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT required in the process to be a senior Maasai warrior?

options.A: Having a part of their bodies removed.
options.B: Showing no signs of fear or pain.
options.D: Staying in the wild with other boys for a night.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the passage about coming-of-age rituals?

options.A: Apache girls dance till they drop in the ceremony.
options.B: The Apache think as long as girls can dance and sing, they can become women.
options.C: The indigenous people in Brazil think the ability of bearing pains decides one’s life and death.
